brief.title: Data Augmentation Effect on CNN Fashion-MNIST Accuracy
brief.summary: This study trains a small convolutional neural network on Fashion-MNIST under two conditions — standard training and training with basic image augmentations — keeping all hyperparameters, architecture, and random seeds identical between conditions. Each condition is run with seeds 42 and 123 for approximately 5 epochs on a CUDA GPU via Google Colab, and test accuracy, training curves, and validation performance are recorded and compared. The goal is to assess whether simple augmentation meaningfully improves generalisation without overstating statistical conclusions given the limited number of seeds.
scope_in: Fashion-MNIST dataset (60 000 train, 10 000 test images)
Two experimental conditions: no augmentation vs. augmentation (random horizontal flip, random crop/translation up to 10%, rotation up to 10°)
One small CNN architecture shared across both conditions
PyTorch implementation with identical optimizer (Adam or SGD), learning rate, batch size, and train/validation split
Training for ~5 epochs per condition per seed
Seeds 42 and 123 for both conditions (4 total runs)
GPU execution on CUDA device (T4 or L4) via Google Colab GPU job tool
Recording of CUDA device detection evidence and per-run metrics
Test accuracy, per-epoch training loss, validation accuracy curves
Summary table and figures comparing conditions across seeds
scope_out: Hyperparameter search or tuning across architectures
Advanced augmentation strategies (CutMix, Mixup, AutoAugment, etc.)
CPU-only fallback training (GPU unavailability is treated as a blocker)
Statistical significance testing beyond descriptive comparison of two seeds
assumptions: Augmentation set chosen as random horizontal flip, random crop (padding 4px), and random rotation (±10°) — common, simple transforms appropriate for clothing images
Adam optimiser assumed unless user specifies otherwise, as it is a standard default for small CNNs
Batch size of 64 assumed as a reasonable default balancing speed and stability
90/10 train/validation split of the 60 000 training images assumed
Small CNN architecture assumed to be 2–3 conv layers with max-pooling followed by 1–2 fully connected layers, keeping training time under 10 minutes per run on a T4
Learning rate of 1e-3 assumed as a standard Adam default
constraints: Must run training on CUDA GPU via Colab; CPU substitution is not permitted
Architecture, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, and split identical between conditions
Must record verifiable GPU evidence (torch.cuda.get_device_name output, device tensors on CUDA)
Do not overstate statistical significance given only two seeds
Use only real computed metrics — no fabricated numbers

clarification.content:
Research question: Does simple data augmentation improve the test accuracy of a convolutional neural network on Fashion-MNIST?

Keep the research relatively simple, scientifically rigorous, and computationally manageable. The study should investigate whether applying basic image augmentation during training improves a CNN's generalization performance compared with training the same CNN without augmentation.

Experimental requirements:
- Dataset: Fashion-MNIST.
- Framework: PyTorch.
- Model: A small CNN suitable for fast training.
- Conditions: Standard training versus training with basic image augmentation.
- Augmentation: Use simple, reasonable transformations such as small random translations or rotations.
- Training: Approximately 5 epochs per condition.
- Random seeds: 42 and 123, for both conditions.
- Keep the architecture, optimizer, learning rate, training/validation split, and other relevant hyperparameters identical between conditions.
- Evaluate test accuracy, training/validation performance, and differences between conditions.
- Generate relevant experimental figures and tables.
- Do not overstate statistical significance with only two seeds.
- Use real literature sources, real computations, and real experimental outputs.
- Compute: the neural network training runs must execute on a CUDA GPU (such as a T4 or L4) through Google Colab using the GPU job tool, and must record verifiable evidence that PyTorch detected the CUDA GPU, that training ran on the CUDA device, and that the reported metrics come from those GPU runs. Do not substitute CPU training. Ordinary Python, data processing and plotting may run in the regular CPU sandbox. If the GPU is unavailable, report that as a blocker rather than changing the experimental requirements.

Keep the project focused. Do not expand it into a large hyperparameter search or extensive benchmark study.

themes.name: CNN Benchmarking on Fashion-MNIST
themes.description: A large body of work uses Fashion-MNIST as a standard testbed for comparing CNN architectures, ranging from classic LeNet-5 to modern residual and attention-based models. These papers establish baseline accuracy ranges and typical architectural choices for the dataset.

themes.name: Effect of Data Augmentation on CNN Generalisation
themes.description: These papers directly investigate whether and how much data augmentation improves CNN classification accuracy, typically comparing augmented versus non-augmented training conditions. They consistently find that basic geometric augmentations reduce overfitting and raise test accuracy, though effect sizes vary by dataset, model, and training length.

themes.name: Augmentation Techniques and Their Specific Impact
themes.description: Studies in this theme focus on specific augmentation operations — flipping, cropping, rotation, circular shift, context placement — and measure their individual or combined contributions. Results suggest horizontal flips and small translations are among the most consistently beneficial basic techniques.

themes.name: Training Dynamics: Hyperparameters, Optimizers, and Batch Size
themes.description: This group examines how training configuration choices such as batch size, optimizer type, and activation function affect CNN performance, providing context for interpreting accuracy differences across training conditions.

themes.name: Lightweight and Efficient CNN Design
themes.description: Several papers focus on building small, parameter-efficient CNNs that remain competitive in accuracy, which is directly relevant to the study's use of a small CNN architecture on a constrained training budget.

themes.name: Data Augmentation in Specialised or Non-Standard Domains
themes.description: These papers apply augmentation to medical images, biological cells, plant leaves, agricultural produce, and handwriting recognition, confirming the generality of augmentation benefits but also highlighting that effect sizes can vary when training data is very scarce or domain-specific.

themes.name: Federated and Privacy-Preserving Learning with Fashion-MNIST
themes.description: A smaller set of papers uses Fashion-MNIST as a benchmark in federated or privacy-preserving learning contexts, relevant primarily as evidence of the dataset's broad adoption as a standard testbed rather than directly addressing augmentation.

overview.summary:
Research on convolutional neural networks for image classification has matured considerably, with Fashion-MNIST emerging as a standard small-image benchmark. Studies consistently show that simple architectural choices (small filters, batch normalization, dropout) combined with basic data augmentation (flips, crops, rotations) can push test accuracy well above 90%, with state-of-the-art results now approaching 99.65% on this dataset. The question of whether augmentation meaningfully helps generalisation is largely answered affirmatively across many domains and datasets, though the magnitude of the benefit depends heavily on training set size, model capacity, and the specific augmentation strategy applied.

For a small CNN trained for only ~5 epochs on Fashion-MNIST's 60,000 images, the benefit of simple augmentation is likely modest but measurable. Most empirical studies find that basic geometric augmentations reduce overfitting and improve test accuracy, especially when training runs are short and model capacity is limited. However, very few studies isolate exactly the experimental design described here (identical architecture, fixed seeds, short training), meaning the field provides directional guidance rather than a precise quantitative prediction for this specific setup.
open_problems: How large is the accuracy gain from simple augmentation specifically for small CNNs trained for only ~5 epochs on Fashion-MNIST, where underfitting rather than overfitting may dominate?
Two seeds (42 and 123) are insufficient for statistical significance testing — it is unclear how much run-to-run variance should be expected and how to interpret small accuracy differences.
Combining multiple augmentation techniques does not always improve over single techniques, and the reasons for this interaction are poorly understood.
Most studies report only final test accuracy rather than training curves, making it hard to understand whether augmentation accelerates or slows early-epoch learning.
Optimal augmentation hyperparameters (flip probability, crop fraction, rotation angle) are rarely tuned systematically; the default values used may not be optimal for a given architecture or dataset.

The relationship between dataset size and augmentation benefit is insufficiently characterised — it is unclear whether Fashion-MNIST's 60,000 training images is large enough that simple augmentation yields only marginal gains.
Generalisation of augmentation findings across datasets remains limited, with most individual studies confined to a single benchmark, making cross-dataset conclusions difficult.

candidates.title: Augmentation benefit direction in 5-epoch underfitting regime

impact.why: Answers a practically important question about when augmentation is worth applying under compute-constrained training.

novelty.why: None of the prior work specifically investigates whether geometric augmentation is neutral or harmful at very short training runs (~5 epochs) versus beneficial at longer runs on Fashion-MNIST with a small CNN; the closest works (e.g., 'State-of-the-Art Results with the Fashion-MNIST Dataset' and 'Multi-Class Image Classification on Fashion-MNIST') use augmentation with longer training schedules (20–100 epochs) without studying the epoch-regime dependency of augmentation benefit.

feasibility.why: Directly extends the core study protocol with only additional epoch-count variants on the same infrastructure.

testability.why: Accuracy at each epoch count is a fully determinate numerical outcome with a clear comparison criterion.

candidates.approach: Run the core 5-epoch protocol for both conditions with seeds 42 and 123, then extend training to 10, 20, and 30 epochs using the same seeds and architecture. Record test accuracy and training/validation loss at each endpoint. Plot the accuracy gap (augmented minus non-augmented) as a function of epoch count to determine whether 5 epochs falls in a regime where augmentation is neutral or harmful and identify the epoch at which consistent benefits first appear.
candidates.question: Does basic geometric augmentation improve or degrade test accuracy of a small CNN trained for only approximately 5 epochs on Fashion-MNIST, where underfitting rather than overfitting is likely to dominate?
candidates.why_open: Studies demonstrating augmentation benefits such as (Çetiner et al. 2023) and (Imam et al. 2026) train models for 50–200 epochs on CIFAR-10 where overfitting dominates, making their results inapplicable to the 5-epoch underfitting regime. (Lin et al. 2023) explicitly shows augmentation can degrade performance when underfitting occurs but does not quantify this effect for Fashion-MNIST or short training budgets. (Guo 2024) shows that even LeNet-5 achieves only 90% validation accuracy on Fashion-MNIST at similar training lengths, suggesting small CNNs operate in a capacity-limited regime where augmentation may introduce harmful noise rather than beneficial regularisation.
candidates.hypothesis: At 5 epochs of training a small CNN on Fashion-MNIST has insufficient capacity utilisation for augmentation to provide a regularisation benefit, resulting in equal or lower test accuracy for the augmented condition, with the benefit emerging only after 15–25 epochs when the non-augmented model begins overfitting.

candidates.title: Ablation of individual augmentation components on Fashion-MNIST

impact.why: Identifying which single augmentation technique provides most benefit avoids unnecessary noise and compute overhead.

novelty.why: A Preliminary Study on Data Augmentation (2019) examines how augmentation method combinations affect CNN classification accuracy and finds that combining two geometric methods can degrade performance—directly relevant to the proposed hypothesis—but does so on different datasets and does not isolate flip, crop, and rotation on Fashion-MNIST in the structured ablation proposed. The specific dataset, architecture, and the full factorial design across all seven conditions remain unaddressed.

feasibility.why: Defining additional training conditions with different torchvision transform pipelines is trivially easy in PyTorch.

testability.why: Each augmentation condition produces a scalar test accuracy making the comparison direct and fully reproducible.

candidates.approach: Define seven augmentation conditions: no augmentation, flip only, crop only, rotation only, flip+crop, flip+rotation, crop+rotation, and all three combined. Run each condition for 5 epochs with seeds 42 and 123 on the same small CNN. Report test accuracy for all conditions in a summary table, compute the marginal contribution of each technique as the accuracy change from adding it to the full combination, and test whether any combination exceeds the best single-technique condition.
candidates.question: When horizontal flip, random crop, and rotation are each applied individually versus in all pairwise and full combinations, which technique drives accuracy gains for a small CNN on Fashion-MNIST at 5 epochs, and does combining techniques improve over the best single technique?
candidates.why_open: (Çetiner et al. 2023) explicitly finds that combining augmentation techniques on CIFAR-10 does not improve over individual techniques and notes the reasons are not analysed. (Korzhebin et al. 2021) confirms that the combination of individually best methods does not necessarily achieve the best combined result but uses only 40 training images. (Shijie et al. 2017) ranks individual augmentation techniques on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet but does not study their interactions or apply them to Fashion-MNIST. No study has performed a systematic single-technique and combination ablation of flip, crop, and rotation specifically on Fashion-MNIST with a small CNN.
candidates.hypothesis: Horizontal flip alone drives the majority of the combined augmentation benefit on Fashion-MNIST because fashion items have meaningful left-right symmetry, while random crop and rotation each add limited additional benefit and their combination with flip produces no statistically meaningful improvement over flip alone.
